title: How to use this course
bridge: A lesson here is like a Playwright spec written with test.step. Given is the picture and the why, When is the code and the lab, Then is the check. Except: here you are the one under test. The last step is a task you finish alone, with no copy to follow.
intro: This course teaches you to build Rhino Health's AI-agent platform yourself, ticket by ticket. There are 242 tickets and 140 lessons. This first lesson shows how every lesson is built and how to work through one. It also shows how to see which tickets you can already do.

picture.caption: One lesson, in the order you meet it on the page.

steps.text: read the bridge, then click Next through the picture, one arrow at a time
read each section: the Why line first, then the code and its numbered notes
run the lab: worked, then faded, then alone
answer three questions and the recall questions from memory
mark the lesson done; its tickets turn to 'You can do this'
pick the next lesson from the ticket you want to do

p: The course has 22 parts. Part p0 is this start. Parts p1 to p12 are foundations: the tools the platform is built with. Examples are Node servers, GitHub Actions, AWS, Temporal and the Claude Agent SDK.

Parts g0 to g8 are walkthroughs, one per goal of the plan. A walkthrough lesson covers a few tickets in build order and explains their code line by line. It ends with the exact steps to do each ticket.
Foundations come first because walkthroughs use them. Every lesson lists the lessons it needs under You need. If a word is new to you, that list tells you where it was taught.

callout.text: You do not have to read every foundation part first. Pick a ticket you want to do, open its lesson, and follow the You need list backwards.

sections.h: Check your tools before the first lab
p: Every lab runs on your laptop with free tools. Most labs need Node 24, git and Docker Desktop. GitHub labs need the gh CLI, logged in to your own account.
Two tools come later: the temporal CLI in part p7 and uv, the Python package manager, in part p10. Install them when you get there.
sections.because: We check the tools first because a wrong Node version is the most common reason a lab fails in a confusing way.

code.text:
node --version                            # the course needs v24.x
npm --version                             # comes with Node
git --version
docker info --format '{{.ServerVersion}}'  # Docker Desktop must be running
gh auth status                            # your own GitHub account

p: A lesson page has four numbered parts. 1 The picture: boxes are things, arrows are what happens, and Next shows one arrow at a time. 2 How it works: the sections. 3 The lab. 4 Check yourself.

Each section starts from something real, a file or a command, and then gives the rule. A Why line comes before every code block and says why the code exists. The numbered notes under the code explain the lines that matter.

After a command you see a You should see box with the exact output. Under it, an If instead line names the most likely error and the fix. Small boxes called Why, Gotcha, Tip and Wall add one point each.

callout.text: A Wall box is a rule enforced by infrastructure, such as 'no keys in the VM'. Walls never change between lessons. If a lesson seems to bend one, the lesson is wrong: tell Sean.

sections.h: The lab ladder: worked, faded, alone
p: Every lab has three tabs. Worked gives every command and what you should see. Faded is the same task with the last step left out. Alone is a new small task of the same shape, with no help.
Type the commands rather than pasting whole blocks. Typing makes you read each flag. When your output differs from You should see, stop and find out why before you go on.

Labs never cost money and never touch a company system or use company credentials. For AWS and other cloud-only things, the lab reads files and dry-runs. That means terraform plan with a local backend, validate, or a local emulator such as LocalStack.
Check yourself has three questions. The wrong options are mistakes people really make, and every option shows one line of why after you pick it. You can change your answer.
Recall asks one or two questions from earlier lessons. Answer them from memory before you scroll back. Pulling a fact out of memory is what makes it stay.
Words lists the new terms of the lesson, at most seven. The same terms, from every lesson, are searchable on the Words page.
The Tickets page shows all 242 tickets by goal. Each ticket shows its team, its days, and the walkthrough lesson that teaches it. A ticket says 'You can do this' once you mark that lesson done.

The counter at the top says 'You can do N of 242'. Only walkthrough lessons move it, because each ticket belongs to exactly one walkthrough lesson. Foundation lessons end with Tickets this unlocks, a short list of tickets that need what you learned.
Your progress lives in this browser's local storage. Another browser or a cleared cache starts from zero.

Every number, path, command and name in the course comes from the tickets, the notes on our real repos, or official docs. When a lesson is not sure of a library detail, it says 'check the docs for X' instead of guessing.
Do the same in your tickets. A guess written down as a fact costs a reviewer more time than an honest open question.

worked.do: Open http://localhost:4310/#/tickets?k=G0-09 and click its lesson link
worked.see: The lesson g0-3 'The independent-approval check', with You need: g0-1, p2-5, p1-6

lab.faded: Find ticket G3-07 on the ticket map the same way. Left to you: open its lesson and read its You need list. Write down every lesson you must finish first. Follow each You need list backwards until you reach p0 or p1.
lab.alone: Pick one goal, for example G4. On the ticket map, count its tickets and add up its days. Then write the three foundation lessons you think you need first. Check your guess against the You need lists of that goal's first two walkthrough lessons.
lab.done: All tool checks print a version and the course runs on localhost:4310. For any ticket, you can find its lesson and the lessons that lesson needs.

quiz.q: A lab step needs an AWS resource. What does the lab ask you to do?

options.text: Log in to the company AWS account with your own user and create it
options.why: Labs never touch company systems or use company credentials.

options.text: Read the code and dry-run it: terraform plan with a local backend, validate, or a local emulator
options.why: That is the rule for every cloud-only step: read and dry-run, never apply.

options.text: Skip the step, because cloud steps cannot be practised on a laptop
options.why: A plan or an emulator shows you what would happen, which is most of the learning.

quiz.q: You mark the foundation lesson p1-6 done. What happens to 'You can do N of 242'?

options.text: It goes up by the tickets p1-6 lists under Tickets this unlocks
options.why: Those tickets belong to walkthrough lessons. The counter follows walkthrough lessons only.

options.text: Nothing: each ticket belongs to one walkthrough lesson, and only those move the counter
options.why: Foundations prepare you; the walkthrough that covers a ticket is what counts.

options.text: It goes up by one, for the lesson itself
options.why: The counter counts tickets, not lessons.

quiz.q: Where is the Why line in a section, and what is it for?

options.text: After the code, as a summary of what it did
options.why: It comes before the code, so you know the reason before you read the lines.

options.text: Before every code block: one sentence that says why we write this code
options.why: Why before how. If you cannot say the why, the code will not stick.

options.text: Only in walkthrough lessons, next to each ticket
options.why: Every code block in every lesson has one.

recall: From your own work: in a Playwright test.step named 'Then ...', what belongs inside it, and what does not?

words.plain: A lesson that teaches a tool the platform uses; it names the tickets it unlocks.
A lesson that covers a few tickets of one goal in build order, with the steps to do each.
One to three sentences: the new thing is like something you know, except for one difference.
The three lab tabs: full example, same task with the last step missing, new task with no help.
A question from an earlier lesson that you answer from memory.
A rule enforced by infrastructure, such as no keys in the VM; it never changes between lessons.
The page with all 242 tickets, the lesson for each, and how many you can already do.

remember: Picture, then Why before code, then a lab you finish alone; the ticket map shows what you can already build.
